analysis.one_liner: Let broadcast companies own more TV stations, newspapers, and cable systems in the same market.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; it died in a House subcommittee with only 11 sponsors, so existing limits on media consolidation stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Federal Communications Commission to relax nearly every rule limiting how many media outlets one company can own. Companies could own two TV stations in the same town, a newspaper and a TV or radio station in the same market, a broadcast station and the local cable system, and more stations nationwide (raising the national reach cap from 35% to 45% of TV households). It would also have let foreign investors from countries that allow American ownership buy into U.S. broadcast licenses. The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Large broadcast and media companies. Relaxing the duopoly, newspaper-broadcast, and cable cross-ownership rules, and raising the national audience cap from 35% to 45%, would let the biggest owners of TV and radio stations and newspaper chains expand into new markets and combine outlets in the same town [S2][S3]. Broadcasters with existing local marketing agreements would have had those arrangements permanently protected [S3]. Foreign investors would gain a path into U.S. broadcast licenses on a reciprocal basis [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let one company own two TV stations in the same market (if at least one is a UHF station, or in unusual cases two VHF stations), and would exempt existing local marketing agreements between stations in the same market from the duopoly rule [S2][S3].

It would order the FCC to eliminate the ban on owning a daily newspaper and a broadcast station in the same market, end the one-to-a-market rule, and prohibit the FCC from limiting ownership of a broadcast station and a cable system serving the same community [S2][S3].
It would raise the national cap on TV audience reach for a single owner from 35 percent to 45 percent, letting major networks own many more stations nationwide [S2][S3].
It would allow broadcast licenses to go to foreign owners from countries that give Americans similar access, capped at 40 percent voting stock [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Viewers and readers in markets where outlets merge. Ownership limits exist to preserve a diversity of local news voices; letting one company own the newspaper, multiple TV stations, and the local cable system concentrates local news and information in fewer hands [S2]. The bill would also have stripped the FCC of discretion to block combinations and required the agency to rewrite its rules within 90 days of enactment, leaving little room to weigh local impacts [S3].

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued the ownership caps were written for a pre-internet, pre-500-channel era and that relaxing them would help struggling UHF stations stay viable and attract foreign capital on a reciprocal basis [S3].

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge the bill ordered the FCC to make all changes within 90 days and barred it from treating a minority stock interest as an ownership stake when one holder controls more than 50 percent, reducing the agency's room to review specific local combinations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered clear, concentrated gains to large media companies and no articulated public benefit mechanism, while removing the main legal checks on one company dominating a local market's newspaper, TV, and cable news. The diversity-of-voices costs were diffuse but real; the gains were concentrated and immediate. As drafted, it was a broad deregulation bill, not a calibrated one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee in March 1999, and neither ever took it up, so it expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on March 2, 1999, joined by six other original sponsors including Democrats Martin Frost and Carrie Meek [S3][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce on the day of introduction, and on March 30, 1999 was referred to its Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote followed, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1][S5].
Ten members cosponsored the bill, split evenly between 5 Democrats and 5 Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing passed, so no company gained anything. The status quo held: the FCC's limits on owning multiple stations, a newspaper and a station, or a station and a local cable system all remained in force, which preserves the wider range of local news voices those rules are meant to protect. Broadcasters hoping to expand had to wait for later deregulation rounds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Local news diversity; broadcasters gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan: a Republican sponsor with an even 5-5 split of Democratic and Republican cosponsors, but the committee of referral took no action either way.

industries.industry: Large broadcast station groups and TV networks
industries.note: Raising the national reach cap to 45% and relaxing the duopoly rule would let the biggest station owners and networks expand in the same market and nationwide. Each additional outlet under common ownership shrinks the number of independent local news voices viewers can choose among.

Eliminating the newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership ban would let a company own the dominant daily paper and a TV or radio station in the same city, combining its news coverage. That concentrates local reporting in fewer hands.
Lifting the ban on owning a broadcast station and the local cable system serving the same community would let broadcasters control both the content and the pipe that delivers it to local homes.

The bill would permanently exempt existing local marketing agreements between same-market stations from the duopoly rule, locking in arrangements where one station effectively runs a nominally competing outlet.
Reciprocal foreign ownership rules would open U.S. broadcast licenses to foreign capital from countries that allow American investment, up to 40 percent voting stock.
